newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: IMF says business as usual with Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: IMF says business as usual with Pakistan.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund will continue negotiations with Pakistan over reviving a stalled $600 million standby loan despite the sacking of Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto, an IMF official said on Tuesday.

President Farooq Leghari sacked Bhutto early on Tuesday, accusing her government of widespread corruption, and named former parliament speaker Meraj Khalid, 80, as interim prime minister pending general elections set for next February 3.

"Our mission is scheduled to be here until the end of the week," the IMF's resident representative in the Pakistani capital, Shamsuddin Tareq, told Reuters. "For the time being we will continue to do work here."

Last week the IMF announced it intended to disburse two delayed tranches, worth about $80 million each, of the $600 million standby loan after approving Bhutto's latest economic stabilisation package.
The IMF had withheld standby loan tranches in June and September because of worries about Pakistan's budget for 1996/97 (July-June).
The withholding of the tranches had compounded economic woes plaguing Bhutto and undermined foreign investors' confidence in Pakistan's finances.
News that the IMF intended to resume assistance to Pakistan sent stocks surging on the Karachi bourse last week.

This week, Pakistan and the IMF mission have been negotiating the terms of a commitment by Islamabad, called a letter of intent, that would clear the way for formal approval of the resumption of IMF lending.
Lending had been expected to resume in late November or early December, Tareq said.
IMF director Paul Chabrier was due to arrive in Islamabad on Tuesday to try to complete the agreement.
Tareq said the mission would continue its technical work in Islamabad despite the sacking of the government. "We have made a lot of progress," he said. "We are close to it (agreement)."

Asked if the dissolution of Bhutto's government would force the mission to change its schedule, Tareq said: "Not as yet. We have to wait and see. We have some work to do, which we are continuing to do, and will see how things emerge."
"We will continue the work we were doing, complete our part of the work, and see what emerges," Tareq said.

Tareq denied reports the two sides had intended to sign the letter of intent this week. He said following talks this week at the technical level, the Pakistani cabinet and IMF management would review the proposed agreement before agreeing to it.
The IMF said last week that the standby loan could be a bridge to a longer-term enhanced structural adjustment facility (ESAF) in fiscal 1997/98.
Pakistan concluded a three-year $1.5-billion ESAF with the IMF that began in February 1994, but payments were suspended a year later because Islamabad failed to achieve many targets.

Last month Pakistan announced an economic stabilisation package that included a 7.86 percent devaluation of the rupee against the dollar as well as spending cuts, new taxes and a 10 percent rise in oil product prices.
This month Bhutto gave up the finance portfolio she had held for three years and named her privatisation chief, Syed Naveed Qamar, as finance minister.
